Seven days in October: Bank of America fined $1.21B, American Express $350M, both for AML failures. Two days after BofA, FIS and Anthropic put an AI investigator on sale to every US bank.
Financial crime compliance is a $40B labour problem. Here is what an agent changes, and what it does not.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗻
→ US banks spend an estimated $35B to $40B a year on AML operations
→ A record 4.1M SARs filed in 2025, up 8%; about 4% get a law enforcement follow-up
→ Up to 95% of monitoring alerts are false positives; investigators spend 40% to 60% of their time collecting evidence

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁
→ Built by FIS on Anthropic's Claude, announced in May, commercial since 15 Oct, open to banks on rival cores too
→ Assembles evidence across core systems, checks typologies, drafts the SAR narrative; every conclusion links to a source record; the analyst decides
→ Runs in FIS's private cloud, native to the Horizon and Systematics cores

𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗮𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗸 ($9.4B assets)
→ Level 1 alert review time: more than 90% less
→ Level 2 case investigation: about 98% less
→ SAR narrative prep: more than 80% less
→ Workflow analysis, not live results yet

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀
→ BofA: $5B+ of suspicious activity unreported, alerts that "failed to escalate" to investigators
→ AmEx: $13B of suspected trade-based laundering over 11 years, "staff without sufficient expertise"

𝗠𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲, from running customer operations
Nobody got fined for slow investigations. They got fined for alerts that never reached an investigator and for teams without the expertise to judge. An agent that compresses evidence-gathering from hours to minutes is worth buying. Using it to cut the people who make the call is buying the next fine.

Banks are drawing a clear line on AI agents.
Use one on your account, and the risk is yours.

TechCrunch reports that Citi updated its online user agreement this week.
Customers who give third-party AI agents access to their accounts are responsible for the activity those agents carry out.
That includes cases where the AI tool leaks credentials or is hacked.

Citi is not alone.
JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October.
PNC changed its terms on November 18.
Wells Fargo goes a step further: from November 24, customers stay liable for an agent's activity unless they can show evidence that they revoked its access, per American Banker.

One detail stands out to me.
Under Citi's terms, the AI agents Citi itself provides come without that extra liability.
So the bank's own agents are welcome. Outside agents are your responsibility.

For companies, two things to watch:
- If you build agents that act on accounts, the platform's terms can decide your product's future.
- If your team uses agents with company logins, read your bank's terms first.

Delegating a task is easy.
Delegating responsibility is not.

Who in your company decides which tools get access to your accounts?

My take: AI contracts are moving from “who” to “who pays”.

This week TechCrunch reported that Citi updated its user agreement. A Citi spokesperson says “customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.” TechCrunch also reported that PNC, JPMorgan and Bank of America have made similar moves.

That’s a consumer story. But I think it’s a preview of every services contract we’ll sign in the next few years.

Here’s how I see the shift.

Old way: we priced the people. Headcount, rate card, SLA. If something broke, the contract already said whose team owned the fix.
AI way: an agent does part of the work, and in my view the hard question becomes who carries the risk when it gets it wrong. The vendor’s agent? The client’s agent? A third-party tool someone plugged in?

Gartner’s Tom Coshow put it well in CIO Dive: “If the vendor isn’t taking on the risk, why are you bothering with outcome-based pricing?”

In my experience running delivery and migration programmes, scope rarely causes the big fights. Unclear ownership does. I’ve seen more time lost arguing “whose problem is this” than fixing the actual issue.

So my simple before/after test for any AI-heavy deal:
Before: “How many people, at what rate?”
After: “When the agent makes a bad call at 2am, whose name is on the fix, and who absorbs the cost?”

If a proposal can’t answer the second one in a sentence, I’d treat the outcome pricing as a label, not a model. That’s my take, not a rule.

When you’ve seen an AI-assisted service go wrong, how did the contract decide who owned it?

Views are my own, not my employer’s.
#AI #ManagedServices #OutcomeBasedPricing #ServiceDelivery #AIAgents

"AI a Hot Potato? Just look at this BofA Survey"

The November 2026 Bank of America (BofA) Global Fund Manager Survey captures a sharp turn in institutional sentiment, treating the AI trade less like a one-way bet and more like a "hot potato" that managers are actively trimming before capital spending slows down.

Why Managers Are Treating AI Like a Hot Potato
20-Year Record Tech Exodus: Net overweight positioning in technology plunged 25 percentage points in a single month—from 37% in October to 12% in November—marking the fastest retreat since June 2006. BofA strategist Michael Hartnett noted bluntly that AI boom euphoria is over and investors are sending a clear signal for companies to pause spending.

Checking the Capex Bill: A record net 38% of respondents say companies are overinvesting in AI.Meanwhile, 52% now expect at least one major AI hyperscaler to announce a capital expenditure (capex) cut within the next six months (up sharply from 30% in October).

Bubble & Credit Stress Dominate Risks: Roughly 65% of surveyed managers flag AI-related threats as the top market tail risk, split between an AI bubble (34%) and an AI hyperscaler credit event (31%)—reflecting growing scrutiny over debt-fueled data center buildouts.

Price Action Confirms the Chill: The survey backdrop coincides with the Nasdaq-100 slipping over 4% in November and semiconductor benchmarks sliding 27% from early October highs, even though "long global semiconductors" remains the single most crowded trade.

Where the Money Is Rotating Instead
Crucially, fund managers are rotating, not retreating into cash—only 3% predict a global recession over the next 12 months, and average cash levels dropped to 3.6%: 

Asset / Region -   November Shift & 2027 Outlook
International Equities - Favored by 36% as the top-performing asset class for 2027, ahead of US equities (24%) and gold (17%).
Europe & India -  Net 67% expect European stocks to rise over the next 1–3 months; managers also turned overweight on India for the first time since January 2026 as an "anti-AI" diversification play.
Defensives & Bonds - Higher allocations to healthcare and consumer staples, while bond underweight positioning was cut by 13 percentage points (largest monthly shift toward bonds since April 2025).
Gold & Currencies - A record net 23% view gold as undervalued near $3,860/oz, while 42% back the Japanese yen to outperform in 2027.

The twist? Big money isn’t hiding in cash. Only 3% expect a recession, and cash levels sit near lows at 3.6%. Instead of exiting risk, institutions are rotating out of crowded US mega-cap tech into international equities (36% top pick for 2027), Europe, healthcare, bonds, and India (back to overweight for the first time since January).
The AI story isn't dead—but the era of "spend at any cost" just hit a wall. Investors are done buying the promise; now they want to see the ROI.

⚠️ If an AI agent gets compromised while interacting with your web app, who holds the bag? According to major US banks this week—the user does.

Over the last 24 hours, Citi, PNC, and Citizens updated their customer terms—following JPMorgan and Bank of America—to shift financial liability for third-party AI agent hacks directly onto account holders. At the same time, Anthropic just closed its historic Nasdaq debut at a $1.3T+ valuation, proving autonomous AI workflows are rapidly becoming standard infrastructure.

When financial liability shifts to the end user, **Frontend UX & Confirmation Design** stops being just "nice to have" and becomes the primary line of consumer protection.
Here is how modern frontend engineering needs to design for high-stakes human oversight:

* 🛑 **Intentional Friction for Destructive or Financial Actions:** We spent a decade optimizing for "1-click" everything. When an AI agent or automated workflow triggers a transfer, permission change, or checkout, UI patterns need deliberate confirmation checkpoints—clear visual diffs showing *what* is changing, *who* initiated it, and *how* to undo it before commitment.

* 🔑 **Passkeys & WebAuthn Over Session Tokens Alone:** When third-party agents act on a user's behalf via delegated sessions, hardware-backed step-up authentication (WebAuthn / Passkeys) inside the browser ensures critical mutations still require cryptographic human presence.

* 🪟 **Transparent Audit Trails in the UI:** Users shouldn't have to dig through raw logs to see what an integrated assistant or extension just did in their session. Surfacing real-time, human-readable activity feeds with TypeScript-enforced action schemas builds trust and catches anomalies before damage spreads.

💡 **Actionable Takeaway:**
Frictionless UX is great for browsing, but **verifiable UX** is essential for transactions. As AI agents take on more user agency, frontend developers are the architects of the final human checkpoint.

Where do you draw the line between seamless automation and intentional UI friction in your apps? Let’s discuss in the comments! 👇

🚀 La notizia AI del giorno · 20 novembre 2026
Bank of America ha pubblicato il suo rapporto 2026 sui titolari di piccole e medie imprese americane: l'84% usa già l'intelligenza artificiale in qualche parte del lavoro. E tra chi la usa, il 94% dice che negli ultimi dodici mesi ha portato almeno un beneficio concreto all'azienda. Il dato più interessante però è un altro: tra chi la usa o sta per usarla, il 52% prevede di assumere persone in più per seguire gli strumenti AI, mentre solo il 33% pensa che ridurrà il personale.
👉 Il punto che conta
Per anni il racconto è stato «l'AI ruba il lavoro». Chi la usa davvero, ogni giorno, racconta una storia diversa: l'AI si prende le ore ripetitive — ribattere ordini, cercare un prezzo, preparare un preventivo — e le persone passano a fare quello che una macchina non fa: seguire il cliente, decidere, vendere. Il 60% dei titolari prevede proprio questo: ruoli nuovi o ridisegnati, non scrivanie vuote.
🔭 Cosa aspettarsi
La differenza non sarà più tra chi usa l'AI e chi no: la usano quasi tutti. Sarà tra chi la usa a pezzi, copiando e incollando in una chat, e chi la mette dentro il proprio lavoro, collegata ai propri dati veri — clienti, listini, magazzino, fatture. Lì il beneficio smette di essere «qualche minuto risparmiato» e diventa un'azienda che corre di più con le stesse persone.
✅ Cosa facciamo noi di Getaweb
1. Partiamo dal lavoro che vi ruba più ore e lo misuriamo, prima di toccare qualsiasi cosa.
2. Mettiamo i vostri dati in un posto solo, il gestionale, perché l'AI lavori su quelli veri.
3. Colleghiamo l'AI a quel gestionale, così le vostre persone la usano dal telefono o dal banco, senza copiare e incollare.
Volete capire dove l'AI può togliervi ore già da questo mese? Contattateci, oppure raccontate il vostro lavoro all'AI di getaweb.it.

Anthropic's Nasdaq debut closed up 17.1%. Asian chip stocks still fell hard.

The market used a record-scale listing to question whether AI spending will earn an adequate return.

Japan's Nikkei 225 fell more than 4% to its lowest level since April. South Korea's KOSPI dropped nearly 5%.

→ The BIS says the five largest hyperscalers were expected to spend more than $1 trillion on AI capex across 2025-26

Reuters commentary noted that most US-designed chips are made outside the US, mainly in Asia.

IMF economist Robert Katz said many AI firms have real earnings growth. The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee called tech valuations stretched.

The money is in. Anthropic priced at $83, opened at $111.50 and raised about $81 billion, the largest IPO on record. 

Amazon and Google backed it early, with roughly $18 billion and $33 billion between them over the years, and now hold stakes worth many times that on paper. 

Wall Street has decided AI is infrastructure.

The accountability is not settled. Citi updated its terms this week: if a customer gives a third-party AI agent access to their account, the customer owns what that agent does.

Misread instructions, unintended actions, even a hack. JPMorgan, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, PNC and Citizens have issued similar terms or warnings.

Here's the detail worth noticing. The banks' own AI agents are exempt. If it's theirs, they stand behind it. If it isn't, you do.

That isn't just a banking story. It's the rule every contact centre is about to live by.
Customers will increasingly reach you through their own AI assistants. And when your AI agent answers, someone has to own what it says and does. Not the model provider. Not the cloud. You.

Three questions worth asking before you put an AI agent in front of customers:

- Can you see every decision it made, on every interaction, not a sample?
- Who in your business signs off on what it is allowed to do?
- When it gets something wrong, how fast do you know, and who fixes it?

Elements of our business at Trusst use Anthropic, so this was a big week for us too. But the model is the engine, not the driver. The outcome your customer gets is the part you own.
Accountability follows ownership.
